title: The One Where Ross Moves In

jokes.text: Joey giggling at a magazine — 'Are you looking at naked tribeswomen?' / 'No, look. That's a pig.' / 'I know. But look at the knobs on it!'
jokes.setup: Joey is giggling at something, implying he's ogling naked women in a magazine.
jokes.punchline: It's a pig — but Joey is admiring its physical attributes ('knobs') with the same leering enthusiasm, revealing his simple-minded nature.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is well-executed — setup implies Joey's being Joey (ogling women), but the punchline reframes it as innocent pig-admiration while still revealing his obliviousness. 'Look at the knobs on it' doing double duty is the key comic engine. Strong character integration: this is quintessential Joey logic.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're not supposed to look at naked women!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because it's wrong!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a pig.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's different then.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, look at the knobs on her!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey!

jokes.text: Ross on being kicked out: 'Who needs a lease when it's family?'
jokes.setup: Joey asks if Ross signed a lease on the apartment he was subletting from his wife's cousin.
jokes.punchline: Ross's rhetorical self-indictment — 'Who needs a lease when it's family?' — reveals his naivety with bitter, well-earned sarcasm.
jokes.explanation: Very economical — one line encapsulates Ross's entire catastrophic decision-making process. The self-awareness makes it land better than a straight complaint would. Fits Ross's character well (overcomplicated life, underestimated trust in social relationships).

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, you didn't get him to sign anything?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, he's my father. I trust him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're an idiot.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Anything you need. But you have to let us know when you feel better so we can make fun of your hair.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey offer sincere support to the freshly homeless/divorced Ross.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately undercuts the sincerity with the caveat that they're reserving the right to mock Ross's hair once the pity window closes.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler: genuine warmth undercut by defensive sarcasm. The 'make fun of your hair' caveat is specific enough to be funny (not just 'make fun of you') and the structure — big offer, then tiny condition — is a reliable but well-executed format. Highly character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm here for you, okay? Whatever you need, I'm gonna be there for you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But right now, you're really bringing down my vibe, so...

jokes.text: Ross says he feels like a 'nomad' — Chandler laughs, then explains to Ross that Joey thought he said 'gonad.'
jokes.setup: Ross laments that he's moved around so much he feels like a 'nomad.'
jokes.punchline: Joey mishears 'nomad' as 'gonad' and finds it hilarious, revealing his juvenile sense of humor via Chandler's explanation.
jokes.explanation: A reliable body-part mishearing gag. The delivery structure — Ross is oblivious, Chandler mediates — is well-suited to these three characters. Joey's childlike giggling adds visual warmth. Not original, but executed with good character specificity. Joey mishearing big words is classic.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean, I'm not tied down to anything. I could move anywhere, do anything.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you're saying you have no gonads?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? No! I said I have no roots!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Right, right. No gonads.

jokes.text: Monica asks if health inspectors work on commission. Larry replies: 'No, bribes.'
jokes.setup: Monica, nervous about Larry's inspection, asks a fumbling question about how he's compensated.
jokes.punchline: Larry deadpans 'bribes' — an unexpected admission that lands as dark self-deprecating humor about the profession.
jokes.explanation: One-word punchline delivered deadpan — maximum economy. The joke works because it simultaneously defuses Monica's anxiety and subverts the expected 'no' answer. Not deeply character-specific but efficiently written.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, did you say gonad?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, he said nomad.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh. What's a nomad?

jokes.text: Monica and Phoebe giggling: 'Larry? Yeah, I'd let him check out my kitchen floor.'
jokes.setup: Larry the health inspector is doing his job in Monica's restaurant. Monica is clearly attracted to him.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's innuendo-laden comment about 'letting him check out her kitchen floor' is delivered as a conspiratorial giggle between friends.
jokes.explanation: Mild innuendo that gets a light giggle. The 'kitchen floor' double entendre is fairly thin and the joke leans on the giggling reaction rather than sharp writing. Functional but not memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So how much do building inspectors make?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, it depends on how many bribes you take.

jokes.text: Larry deducts two points from Monica's score for not wearing her hat — then tricks her into going into the kitchen without it, watches her go get it hatlessly, and declares: 'Ah, there's the two points! You should really read that book you wrote.'
jokes.setup: Monica brags that she 'wrote the book on Section 5' and that you only need to wear the hat in the kitchen. Larry deducts two points for the hat violation.
jokes.punchline: Larry has engineered the trap all along — he knew she'd walk into the kitchen without her hat. 'You should really read that book you wrote' is the perfect ironic kicker.
jokes.explanation: This is a legitimately well-constructed bit. It has a setup (Monica's boast), a trap (Larry engineering her violation), and a perfect kicker that uses her own words against her. The callback to 'wrote the book on Section 5' makes the punchline feel earned rather than imposed. Strong structure — better than the average Friends joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not trying to bribe you or anything, but if you could just overlook this one little thing...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Did you just...?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, no, no! I meant— that came out wrong. I was just saying—

jokes.text: Phoebe, admiring Larry's cunning: 'You saw the hat in the kitchen and knew she'd go in hatless to get it.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just sprung his inspection trap on Monica.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe narrates the scheme back to Larry with breathless admiration, as if he's Sherlock Holmes — the joke is in the over-reverent tone for such a mundane health inspector trick.
jokes.explanation: The humor comes from Phoebe's disproportionate admiration for a pretty simple trick. It amplifies the previous joke's impact but doesn't stand alone particularly well. Phoebe's wide-eyed earnestness is well-used here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm actually very clean. I shower like, once a week.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's not clean.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I also use a lot of perfume. And I sleep naked on top of my sheets, which I wash... occasionally.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you're basically a health code violation waiting to happen.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I've never gotten sick. That means my immune system is strong!

jokes.text: Phoebe suggests Larry could have his own detective show — and pitches herself as his sidekick, 'Voonda.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is starstruck by Larry's inspection technique.
jokes.punchline: She leaps to pitching a TV show and has already named her character 'Voonda' — the specificity of the fake name is the comedic kicker.
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe-specific — only she would already have her sidekick alter ego named. 'Voonda' is a funny, specific, slightly exotic invented name that feels right for Phoebe's brand of whimsy. The joke escalates naturally from her admiration of Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: According to my book, you should always maintain proper ergonomic posture while sitting.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you're slouching.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm an exception to my own rules.

jokes.text: Rachel says she doesn't go for guys right after a divorce. Monica: 'Right, you only go for them five minutes before they get married.'
jokes.setup: Rachel declares she won't pursue Ross because she 'doesn't go for guys right after they get divorced.'
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately calls out Rachel's real pattern — pursuing men who are about to get married — referencing Rachel's history (most notably running from her own almost-wedding and her complicated history with Ross).
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. It's perfectly economical, deeply character-specific (this requires you to know both Rachel and Monica's histories), and the punchline lands like a precision strike. Monica's ability to weaponize truth as a comeback is her core comedic mode, and this is a great example. The audience who knows the show's history feels rewarded. Comfortably in the 8-range.

jokes.text: After Danny invites them to his party and leaves, Monica deadpans: 'So I guess we won't be warming his house.'
jokes.setup: Danny invited the group to his party but conspicuously did not ask Rachel out — Rachel was hoping for more.
jokes.punchline: Monica's dry observation that this party invitation is not a romantic invitation undercuts Rachel's flirtatious expectations.
jokes.explanation: A quick dry line with a mild laugh. The 'warming his house' wordplay on 'housewarming' is functional but understated. Monica's deadpan delivery would carry it on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you should totally have your own detective show! Like, 'Law & Order: Special Phoebe Unit.'

jokes.text: Rachel's elaborate theory about Danny's party invitation — concluding 'Blew up in his face, didn't it? Ha.' — followed by Monica's confused 'So there is no party?' / Rachel: 'No, there's a party. There's a party.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has constructed an elaborate psychology about Danny's party invite — he did it to get her to hint for an invitation, but she didn't take the bait, so power is hers.
jokes.punchline: Monica's flat 'So there is no party?' punctures the whole tortured analysis. Rachel's earnest 'No, there's a party. There's a party' makes it worse — she's outsmarted nothing.
jokes.explanation: Monica's one confused question demolishes Rachel's entire self-congratulatory theory. The humor lies in the absurdity of Rachel's power-game logic collapsing with one practical question. Well-structured comic deflation. Monica as reality-check straight-woman is perfect here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You should write a detective show.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A detective show? Like what, 'Phoebe and Watson'?

jokes.text: Joey, trying to follow Rachel's elaborate game theory, finally summarizes: 'So he won't invite you to his party because he likes you?' Rachel: 'Exactly!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has spent several lines explaining her intricate theory of romantic power dynamics to Monica and Joey.
jokes.punchline: Joey strips her convoluted logic down to its absurd core — and Rachel validates his reductive summary with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: A great double-character joke: Joey's simplification is funny because it's accidentally accurate AND because it reveals how ridiculous the whole theory is. Rachel's 'Exactly!' — said with complete sincerity — is the perfect button. Very economical, good use of both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So what do you do?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm a masseuse.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, that's nice. Do you have any restaurant recommendations?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I give a lot of rubdowns, so I know where all the sore spots are in the city.

jokes.text: Ross plays his new answering machine message: a parody of Queen's 'We Will Rock You' — 'We will, we will call you back.'
jokes.setup: Joey mentions Ross could put his name on the answering machine since he'll be staying a while.
jokes.punchline: Ross has already 'jazzed it up' with an enthusiastically terrible Queen parody that only he would think was cool.
jokes.explanation: Peak Ross Geller. Only Ross — the dorky, earnest, emotionally oblivious professor — would respond to moving into his friends' apartment by immediately 'jazzing up' the answering machine with an a cappella Queen parody. The character integration is exceptional. The image of Chandler and Joey's forced polite laughter ('the tears are real') is funny on its own. This bit is a small classic of Ross-ness.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't go for recently divorced guys.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, you go for engaged ones.

jokes.text: Chandler and Joey are fake-laughing at the answering machine. Joey: 'You're fake laughing too, right?' Chandler: 'The tears are real.'
jokes.setup: Ross's terrible answering machine message plays. Both Chandler and Joey perform polite chuckles.
jokes.punchline: Joey checks in with Chandler that they're both faking it; Chandler's 'The tears are real' implies the message is so bad it's caused genuine emotional distress.
jokes.explanation: 'The tears are real' is one of the best lines in the episode — four words that imply a universe of suffering. It's maximally economical, perfectly in Chandler's voice, and lands with genuine wit. The setup (Joey checking if they're both fake-laughing) makes the punchline land harder. This is what a great Chandler line looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I was totally flirting with him! I mean, I touched his arm, I laughed at his jokes, I even did that thing where I tilt my head and look interested.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He was eating it up! I could tell he was completely into me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Then he said, 'Well, it was nice meeting you,' and walked away.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Turns out he was just being polite because I was standing between him and the snack table.

jokes.text: Larry shuts down the restaurant: 'I saw ten violations. I'm shutting this place down!' Monica: 'You have the power to do that?' Larry: 'This does.' [holds up badge]
jokes.setup: Monica has been charmed by Larry all evening, treating his health inspection like a date.
jokes.punchline: The restaurant gets shut down — Larry is simultaneously her date and the person professionally destroying her livelihood, and Monica's shocked question reveals she hadn't connected those dots.
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is good — Monica's romantic haze blinded her to the professional danger Larry posed. The badge callback ('This does') ties it together. A solid end-of-scene punctuation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could she BE any more obvious?

jokes.text: Chandler catches Joey building a fort in the living room out of the couch cushions.
jokes.setup: Chandler comes home to find Joey doing something suspicious.
jokes.punchline: Joey has built a blanket/cushion fort — a child's activity — and doesn't deny it. The humor is in the domestically regressed behavior being treated as completely normal.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Joey — he has the emotional and intellectual development of a large child. The fort is a funny visual. The 'Kind of, heh' half-admission is well-played. Not especially original but character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, he didn't invite us to his housewarming party? That is so rude!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, maybe he's planning to warm up the house himself.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh please. The only thing Danny's warming up is his reputation as a jerk.

jokes.text: Chandler discovers Ross's air purifier — 'All I heard for four years through college was [humming].' Joey: 'You should have gone out once in a while.'
jokes.setup: Ross's air purifier is running loudly in the apartment; Chandler reacts with horror.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's story of four years of college suffering from the purifier's hum is punctuated by Joey's aside that the solution was simply to 'go out once in a while' — implying Chandler and Ross were equally homebody nerds.
jokes.explanation: Joey's aside is the best part — it's a mild dig at both Chandler and Ross for being college shut-ins. Good economy; the humming bit sells it physically. Builds the 'Ross is an annoying roommate' thread effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So Danny's plan was to fail at something that would actually help him succeed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And now he's celebrating because it worked.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Come watch TV in the fort.' — said as a straight-faced grownup convincing Ross's friend to do something he initially complained about.
jokes.setup: Chandler was complaining about the air purifier and Ross being annoying. Joey appeals to his sense of loyalty.
jokes.punchline: Joey convinces Chandler to 'be a grownup' — and the grownup solution is to watch TV in a blanket fort.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the juxtaposition: Joey invokes maturity to get Chandler to do something profoundly immature. 'Come watch TV in the fort' is a funny callback because it makes the fort sound like a legitimate domestic arrangement.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, if he likes me, he'll wait. And if he doesn't like me, then I don't want him anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So... you want him to like you?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No! I want him to wait!

jokes.text: Rachel claims she's busy — 'I've got a gala.' Danny: 'What's the gala for?' Rachel: 'It's a... regatta gala.' Danny: 'Do you sail?' Rachel: 'No, but I support it.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is trying to look unavailable and play the power game, so she invents a fake prior engagement.
jokes.punchline: The lie compounds hilariously — 'regatta gala' is an absurd specific detail, and 'No, but I support it' is the perfect, increasingly desperate improvised justification.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier cringe bits in the episode. Each question Danny asks makes Rachel's lie more elaborate and absurd. 'Regatta gala' is a great specific-sounding nonsense phrase, and 'No, but I support it' is quotable and funny because it simultaneously sounds reasonable and completely inadequate. Well-constructed escalating cringe.

jokes.text: 'Remember? I've got that, uh, gala.' / 'What's the gala for?' / 'It's a, um... it's a regatta gala.' / 'Do you sail?' / 'No, but I support it.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has invented a fake event to avoid admitting she has nothing better to do.
jokes.punchline: Under Danny's questioning, the lie escalates: gala → regatta gala → 'I don't sail, but I support it.' Each answer is more absurd than the last.
jokes.explanation: 'No, but I support it' is a genuinely excellent line — the specificity of 'regatta' and the helpless commitment to the increasingly implausible lie is very Rachel. The escalation structure is well-executed: each beat raises the stakes of her absurdity. Character integration is high — this exact flavor of panicked improvised snobbery is Rachel's signature.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was painful.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe he said that.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We have to tell him.

jokes.text: Joey randomly slaps something [sound effect] during Rachel's power-game monologue. Monica: 'Joey, please.' Joey: 'Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has resumed her complicated analysis of the dating power game after Danny leaves.
jokes.punchline: Joey is so disengaged from Rachel's theorizing that he has apparently started hitting something nearby — the slapping sound is the comedic beat, with Monica's weary 'Please' and Joey's sheepish 'Sorry' confirming the visual.
jokes.explanation: A quick physical comedy beat — Joey can't focus during Rachel's lengthy monologue and starts restlessly making noise. It's character-consistent and breaks the monologue nicely. More of a live-audience laugh than a rewatch laugh.

dialogue.line: Sexual innuendo about the badge's history

jokes.text: Buzzing noise from somewhere in the apartment — Ross apparently screams (the [SCREAMS] beat at 09:30) in what appears to be a comedic overreaction inferred from context.
jokes.setup: Ross is living with Chandler and Joey and already a source of domestic disruption (the air purifier).
jokes.punchline: Ross's scream — presumably at something mundane — plays as an outsized reaction, adding to the 'Ross as disruptive houseguest' thread.
jokes.explanation: Hard to fully evaluate without the visual. The buzzing-then-screaming beat is a physical slapstick moment but it's entirely dependent on what Ross does on screen. As written, it's a placeholder — likely funnier in execution than on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: This has been really nice, Larry. I feel like we have a real connection.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I know. I've never felt this way before.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So... what happens now?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, I should probably tell you - I'm your waiter, and there's a table of eight who just sat down in my section.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'll be right back.

jokes.text: Ross appears asking if anyone wants to play foosball — but Joey has moved the table into his room 'because of all the boxes.'
jokes.setup: Ross wants to play foosball — an easy social activity for the three of them.
jokes.punchline: The foosball table has been moved to Joey's room because Ross's boxes are taking over the apartment — illustrating that Ross's presence is already reorganizing their space.
jokes.explanation: A quiet bit of situational comedy — Ross's disruption of the apartment is shown rather than stated. Functions well as scene business but isn't a memorable joke on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, fine! I was building a fort.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A fort? Joey, you're thirty years old.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know how old I am!

jokes.text: 'We moved the table into my room because of all the boxes.' — the foosball table has been displaced by Ross's boxes.
jokes.setup: Ross wants to play foosball and suggests they all go play.
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals that he already displaced their foosball table with his stuff — and is now asking to play it in the room he commandeered.
jokes.explanation: The obliviousness of Ross not registering that displacing their foosball table is an imposition — while asking to play it — is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What is that noise?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, that's my new humidifier.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your humidifier sounds like it's humidifying a chainsaw. Could it BE any louder?

jokes.text: Ross's hand gesture — 'Bye-bye, little puppet Joey hand' — Chandler asks about the 'quiet down' gesture, Ross explains, Chandler reveals Ross taped over his Baywatch tape with a bug documentary.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are cataloguing the annoying things Ross has introduced into their apartment.
jokes.punchline: Ross has a 'quiet down' hand gesture (apparently an odd tic), and has also taped over Chandler's Baywatch tape with a bug documentary — each detail more eccentric than the last.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of Ross-as-annoying-houseguest: first a weird gesture, then a tape-over incident. The specificity of 'bugs' replacing 'Baywatch' is funny — not generic programming, but something that feels very Ross (scientist, nature enthusiast) versus very Chandler/Joey (swimsuit show).

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can hear that thing through college. It's like living next to a jet engine.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So don't listen to it.

jokes.text: 'Bye-bye, little puppet Joey hand?' — Joey mistakes Chandler's Ross impression for a puppet show.
jokes.setup: Chandler is demonstrating Ross's annoying hand gesture.
jokes.punchline: Joey thinks Chandler's gesturing hand is a puppet and says goodbye to it — revealing Joey's complete failure to understand what's happening.
jokes.explanation: 'Bye-bye, little puppet Joey hand' is a great Joey line — it's exactly the kind of childlike, oddly specific non sequitur that makes Joey funny. The character integration is excellent: only Joey would interpret a hand gesture as a puppet show and address it warmly. It's also a good line to say out loud.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on, Chandler, you gotta grow up. Be more mature.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're right, you're right. I'll be more responsible from now on.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's great! Hey, you wanna build a fort out of couch cushions?

jokes.text: Joey: 'My God! What if that had been porn?' — reacting to Ross taping over Chandler's Baywatch tape.
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals Ross taped over his Baywatch tape with a bug documentary.
jokes.punchline: Joey leaps to the worst-case scenario — what if it had been porn? — revealing that for Joey, the real tragedy would be losing pornography, not a swimsuit show.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Joey. His priority hierarchy (pornography > Baywatch > everything else) is instantly recognizable. The delivery is funny because it's genuinely horrified, not ironic. Short, economical, completely character-specific. Gets a solid laugh from the studio audience and from viewers who know Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, did you see? Churman's has vermin violations!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I guess it's not Churman's anymore... it's Verman's!

jokes.text: After Joey and Chandler lose at foosball (presumably badly), they immediately agree Ross should leave: 'So he's out of here. Mm-hm.'
jokes.setup: Chandler was persuaded by Joey to tolerate Ross; they play foosball in Joey's room (with Ross presumably beating them).
jokes.punchline: The foosball loss is apparently the last straw — they silently agree Ross must go. The speed of the reversal (from 'I'll hold out a little longer' to instant eviction planning) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the cutaway — we don't see what happened, just the aftermath: total reversal of position in apparently seconds. The 'Mm-hm' confirmation is funny in its resigned certainty. Good comic economy.

jokes.text: Monica, asked where to eat now that Larry has shut down their favorite places: 'I don't know. Clean places?' Chandler: 'Mm, yum!'
jokes.setup: Larry has been shutting down restaurants around the group, leaving them without their usual spots.
jokes.punchline: Monica's straight answer — 'clean places' — is funny because it implies their favorite places have been health hazards all along, and Chandler's unenthusiastic 'Mm, yum' confirms that cleanliness sounds less appealing than familiar filth.
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat exchange. Monica's straight line is funny ('clean places' as a novel concept), and Chandler's 'Mm, yum!' punctuates it perfectly — his deadpan disgust at the idea of hygienic food is wonderfully absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You gotta treat dating like a sport, y'know? You warm up, you get in the game, you score...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, I'm not a touchdown.

jokes.text: Rachel, panicked about Danny seeing her when she's supposed to be at a gala: 'What kind of a regatta gala starts at night?' Monica: 'The fake kind.'
jokes.setup: Danny knocks on the door while Rachel is home — she's supposed to be at an invented 'regatta gala.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's calm, devastating 'The fake kind' reduces Rachel's entire scheme to its obvious absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Three words: 'The fake kind.' Perfect callback, perfect economy. Monica's ability to cut through Rachel's self-delusion is a core comedic dynamic of their friendship. The punchline is so clean and efficient it's near-ideal. Comfortably the best Monica line in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know, but apparently it's worth a lot of money.

jokes.text: 'You know what Larry would say? He'd say, See you ladle.' [LAUGHS]
jokes.setup: Danny has borrowed a ladle and is leaving. Phoebe is still starstruck by Larry the health inspector.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe invents a Larry-ism — 'See you ladle' instead of 'See you later' — a terrible pun she finds hilarious, consistent with her childlike delight in wordplay.
jokes.explanation: It's a dad-joke-level pun, but Phoebe's delight in bad wordplay is so character-consistent that it earns a laugh through performance rather than quality writing. The pun itself is weak, but Phoebe owning it is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You taped over my Baywatch tape?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I needed to tape the Discovery Channel special.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ross! Do you understand what you've done? That tape is irreplaceable!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, it's just a TV show. You can buy another copy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's not just a TV show! I was on that tape! Well, I mean... I was watching it... but still!

jokes.text: Ross with the newspaper: 'I'm done. You want anything? Sports? International? Apartment listings?' — then claims both Sports AND International because 'I'm Italian.'
jokes.setup: Ross is reading the newspaper at Chandler and Joey's; he offers to leave sections for them.
jokes.punchline: Ross takes BOTH Sports and International, with the flimsy justification 'I'm Italian' — a non-sequitur that reveals he has no self-awareness about hogging everything.
jokes.explanation: Ross's 'I'm Italian' is funny as a non-sequitur excuse — he isn't particularly Italian, it's a vague claim used to justify claiming entire newspaper sections. Good character work: Ross's obliviousness to his own imposition on others is a recurring theme this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Living with Ross is like an endurance test. I wake up, I think, 'Will today be the day he finally leaves me alone?' Spoiler alert: it's not.

jokes.text: Chandler steers Ross toward the apartment listings, specifically to the circled expensive studio — 'it's available now,' said with barely-concealed desperation.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey have decided Ross needs to leave. They guide his newspaper reading toward the apartment listings.
jokes.punchline: The subtle engineering — 'What about that circled one?' — reveals they've pre-circled an apartment listing, making the whole newspaper-sharing scene a manipulation setup.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that they pre-circled the apartment is a good structural joke — it recontextualizes the whole newspaper scene as an elaborate scheme. Joey and Chandler's attempts at casual manipulation are funnier because they're obviously clumsy about it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh great! A health inspector closing restaurants? Finally, someone's looking out for us! You know what this means? Clean food! Joey Tribbiani eating clean food. That's like... that's like asking me to act in a Shakespeare play without saying 'how you doin'?' It ain't gonna happen, people!

jokes.text: Ross asks if they'll 'chip in for new air filters for the purifier' as they're rushing him out the door to look at apartments. Chandler: 'Let's go quicker!'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are barely containing their excitement about getting Ross out of the apartment.
jokes.punchline: Ross — obliviously — tries to get them to invest in his air purifier at the exact moment they're trying to eject him. Chandler's 'Let's go quicker!' breaks the barely-civil pretense.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the air purifier gag, now escalated to Ross trying to monetize it. 'Let's go quicker' as Chandler barely keeping the scheme together is a nice character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're telling me you flew to Paris, had dinner with him, and flew back the same night?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's like a 14-hour flight each way. When exactly did you sleep?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I made it up. Are you happy now?

jokes.text: Chandler reacts to the apartment's combined kitchen/bathroom: 'That's great! So you can cook while in the tub. Somebody was using his head.'
jokes.setup: The apartment they've brought Ross to see has an absurd floor plan — kitchen and bathroom are the same room.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's deadpan endorsement of the nightmare kitchen/bathroom combo — 'you can cook while in the tub!' — is sarcastic cheerleading for a terrible apartment they want Ross to take anyway.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's deadpan spin-doctoring of a horrifying apartment is very funny. 'Cook while in the tub' as a selling point is absurdist, and 'somebody was using his head' is a great ironic kicker. The joke works doubly — as apartment humor and as evidence of how desperate they are to place Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Ladle!

jokes.text: Ross goes downstairs to fill out the application. Chandler: 'We are bad people.' Joey: 'He knew we were trying to get rid of him.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey have successfully maneuvered Ross into applying for an apartment they clearly steered him toward.
jokes.punchline: Their instant moral collapse — and the kicker that Ross apparently KNEW the whole time — transforms the scheming from clever to embarrassingly transparent.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal: they think they've been subtle; Ross knew. The 'We are bad people' confession is funny in its immediacy. Joey's revelation that Ross was onto them makes the whole scheming sequence retroactively funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There's nothing in the listings.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What do you mean there's nothing? There's gotta be something.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, I'm telling you, there's nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, keep looking! There's always something hidden in the back pages or... or online, or...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, I've looked everywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Maybe there's a secret apartment. Like, behind a wall or something.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Could we get a bathtub in our kitchen?'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey have just finished maneuvering Ross into a terrible apartment with a kitchen/bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, apparently genuinely charmed by the kitchen/bathroom concept he was mocking seconds ago, sincerely asks if they could do the same.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the apartment scene. Chandler was mocking the kitchen/bath with sarcasm, but the joke turns on him genuinely wanting it. The hypocrisy is funny; the earnestness of the question is funnier. Great economy — one line, complete thought, good laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could this apartment BE any smaller? I mean, look at this—the kitchen and bathroom are basically the same room.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But hey, think about it—you could be brushing your teeth and cooking breakfast at the same time. Really cuts down on multitasking!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Plus, if you drop your toast, it's only three steps to the toilet. Very efficient.

jokes.text: The group wants to go to Monica's restaurant (closed by Larry) and several others — each one crossed off. The host claims the displayed milk is fresh: 'I bought this today because I was thirsty for milk, you know?' — then gags on it.
jokes.setup: Larry has been shutting down restaurants; Monica tries to defend a diner by claiming its milk is fresh.
jokes.punchline: The host's overly specific defense ('I was thirsty for milk, you know?') and immediate gagging on the milk is a perfect slapstick punctuation — the lie is exposed by the liar's own body.
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy escalation: verbal lie → physical comedy disproof. 'I was thirsty for milk, you know?' is a great anxious over-justification. The gag has good pacing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I love what you've done with the place! This is really... something.

jokes.text: Larry cites 'Health Code 11 B' requiring refuse go out the back exit; sanitation worker protests it's inconvenient; Larry: 'So you choose convenience over health?'
jokes.setup: Larry has been shown to cite specific codes obsessively.
jokes.punchline: His completely righteous framing of a minor trash disposal preference as a moral choice — 'you choose convenience over health?' — is an absurd escalation of bureaucratic authority.
jokes.explanation: Larry as power-mad inspector is a consistent joke. This is a functional entry in that gag — not especially inventive but continues to characterize him as someone who can't turn off the job.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So what do you guys think? Should I take the apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, it's a great place, but there's one small problem.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You live there.

jokes.text: Monica tells Larry to stop being 'Larry the health inspector guy' and just be Larry: 'It was exciting at first. But now it's like, so where are we going to eat ever?'
jokes.setup: Larry is about to bust the trash-taking man for a health code violation.
jokes.punchline: Monica breaks down their relationship dynamic — she was charmed by his authority, now realizes it's making dining impossible. The 'where are we going to eat EVER?' desperation is funny in its escalation.
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Monica's control-freak perfectionism is usually applied to cleanliness, but here it conflicts with her desire for good food. 'Where are we going to eat ever' has nice desperation. The scene serves the running gag well.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We feel terrible about what we did.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, we basically tricked you into taking that apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're really sorry, Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? You guys manipulated me?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We knew you wouldn't take it otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And we feel awful about it.

jokes.text: Monica, negotiating Larry to give the trash guy a warning: 'If after dinner you still need to bust someone, I know a hot dog vendor who picks his nose.'
jokes.setup: Larry is about to cite the trash man; Monica is trying to redirect his enforcement instincts.
jokes.punchline: Monica offers a consolation bust — a nose-picking hot dog vendor — as if she's managing an addict: 'you can have a little, just not now.' The specificity of the alternative is funny.
jokes.explanation: Funny in its specificity and in the way Monica manages Larry like he's an enforcement-addicted toddler. The nose-picking hot dog vendor is a vivid, specific image that sells the joke. Good comic economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what? I've been thinking about your apartment situation, and you know what? I got an idea. What if we knock down that wall between your bedroom and your living room?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, that's a load-bearing wall.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So? We'll get Chandler to help us. He's pretty strong.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, Joey, if we knock down a load-bearing wall, the building will collapse.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh. Well... could we at least paint it a nice color?

jokes.text: No closet space in the apartment — Chandler: 'No closet space, but he could hang his stuff out the window in a bag.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are reflecting on the apartment they steered Ross toward.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, still spin-doctoring, presents hanging clothes out the window in a bag as a viable solution to no closet space — delivered with the same cheerful deadpan as his kitchen/bath endorsement.
jokes.explanation: Continuation of Chandler's running deadpan spin on the terrible apartment. 'In a bag' is the key detail that makes it funny — it's weirdly specific and genuinely absurd. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So you're telling me the health inspector found nothing wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's right. He said it was the cleanest restaurant he'd ever seen. He actually ate here. Twice.

jokes.text: Chandler answers the apartment manager's reference call for Ross — starts positive, then tries to sabotage him with increasingly absurd claims: big barking dog → tap dancer → pimp.
jokes.setup: Ross put Chandler and Joey as references on his apartment application; the manager calls.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's sabotage escalates from plausible (dog) to absurd (tap dancer) to inexplicable (pimp), with Joey helpfully chiming in 'He's a pimp!' and Chandler's 'There you go. He's a big, tap-dancing pimp!'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The escalation is brilliantly structured: each sabotage claim is more absurd than the last (dog → tap dancer → pimp), and the apartment manager's apparently unflappable responses ('some would say that is a lost art') make it funnier. 'He's a big, tap-dancing pimp!' is a perfect peak absurdity line. The collaborative chaos between Chandler and Joey — Chandler structured, Joey blurting — is great character comedy. Comfortably above the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Can't you just be a person for five minutes? Not a health inspector, just a person?

jokes.text: Apartment manager's response to 'He's a tap dancer': 'Yes, some would say that is a lost art.' Chandler is derailed — his sabotage isn't working.
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to destroy Ross's application with increasingly absurd claims; the manager takes each one in stride.
jokes.punchline: The manager treating 'tap dancer' as a thoughtful cultural observation rather than a disqualifying character flaw completely undermines Chandler's scheme.
jokes.explanation: The apartment manager's deadpan open-mindedness is what makes the escalation work. 'Some would say that is a lost art' is a genuinely funny line — it's so reasonable and culturally appreciative that it's absurd. Part of what makes joke 43 work as a whole.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hey Larry, instead of inspecting me, why don't you inspect that guy over there? I'm pretty sure he's violating several health codes just by existing.

jokes.text: Monica tells Rachel to distract Danny — 'But don't be sexy.'
jokes.setup: Rachel needs to get back upstairs as if she's returning from her fake gala; Monica sends her to distract Danny.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't be sexy' — Monica's warning implies that Rachel's default mode IS sexy, and they need specifically the un-sexy version of Rachel right now.
jokes.explanation: Quick, punchy, character-specific. The implication that Rachel being 'not sexy' requires a specific instruction is funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, you don't have a closet? What do you do with your clothes?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I keep them in a garment rack... and some boxes under the bed.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, that's fine. That's totally normal. I'm sure lots of people store their entire wardrobe under their bed like it's a dead body.

jokes.text: Joey distracts Danny by intensely quizzing him about the food at his party — 'Most parties, it's all chips and salsa, chips and salsa' — then literally pointing at dishes: 'What's this?' 'Salad.' 'And what's this?' 'Bread.' — Danny: 'Aren't you a chef?' Joey: 'Oh.'
jokes.setup: Monica has told Joey to distract Danny so Rachel can sneak upstairs. Joey's distraction technique is to interrogate Danny about his food.
jokes.punchline: Joey's questioning reveals he is so genuinely excited about the party food that he doesn't even recognize a salad or bread — and when Danny asks 'aren't you a chef?', Joey is caught out. 'Oh.' is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Joey. His obsessive focus on food overrides his ability to accomplish any task — he forgets he's supposed to be distracting Danny and just becomes genuinely absorbed in the food question. The 'Aren't you a chef?' callback (Joey was supposedly a chef or food-aware person) and his simple 'Oh.' makes it land well.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: He's a paleontologist.

jokes.text: Rachel returns from her fake gala, breezes in: 'Oh right, tonight was your party.' After Danny says he's glad she made it and doesn't want her to leave: 'Whose court is the ball in now?' / Monica: 'I thought there wasn't a ball.' / Rachel: 'Ball's flying all over the place.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been using sports metaphors throughout the episode to describe her power games with Danny ('ball in his court').
jokes.punchline: Earlier Rachel insisted 'there's no ball' — now that things are going her way, 'ball's flying all over the place.' Monica's callback to the ball denial is the sharp jab.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the ball/sports metaphor running gag. Rachel's hypocrisy is well-exposed — she disowned the metaphor when it didn't serve her, reclaimed it immediately when it did. Monica's one-line callback is sharp. The escalating absurdity of 'Ball's flying all over the place' as a confident victory lap is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I also have a son. He's very quiet, never gets in anyone's way.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: That's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And I do a lot of heroin.

jokes.text: Danny introduces Rachel to his friend Tom: 'This is the girl I told you about.' Rachel: 'Oh come on! You telling people about me?' — but then Danny sets Tom up with Rachel and goes to 'mingle.'
jokes.setup: Danny introduces Rachel to his friend Tom, apparently having told Tom about her — Rachel takes this as proof of romantic interest.
jokes.punchline: Danny is setting Tom up with Rachel, not declaring his feelings — the 'told you about me' is about matchmaking, not pursuing. Rachel's confident 'come on!' makes the reversal land harder.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — Rachel reads the situation completely wrong in real time, and the audience sees the reversal a beat before she does. Her confident preening ('you telling people about me?') makes the humiliation funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: That was beautiful tap dancing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: You know, I'm gonna give you a raise.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, really?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: No, I'm just kidding. But I am gonna let you leave work early today.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, that's nice, but I was kind of hoping for the raise.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: Tell you what — if you tap dance for me every day, I'll consider it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Every day? I'm gonna have to rob a bank.

jokes.text: Rachel to Tom, cutting through his small talk: 'At ease, soldier. I'm sorry? You can just drop the act. I know what's going on. You're Danny's wingman, right? You guys are best buds, frat bros.'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to make polite conversation; Rachel has deduced he's Danny's operative.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's military metaphors and fraternity vocabulary applied to a mundane party introduction are absurdly overblown — she's treating a housewarming party like a spy thriller.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's escalating paranoia about the Danny situation is well-characterized here. 'At ease, soldier' is a funny overcorrection. The comic engine is Rachel's completely disproportionate response to ordinary small talk.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross? Yeah, he's a vampire. He only comes out at night, he's afraid of crosses, and he has an irrational fear of garlic bread.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, so Ross is a vampire who's afraid of garlic bread? That's like being a firefighter who's afraid of fire.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, also he once told me he was bitten by a radioactive bat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, so Ross is a vampire firefighter who got bitten by a radioactive bat and he's afraid of garlic bread? No wonder he and Rachel didn't work out.

jokes.text: Rachel dismisses Tom: 'I'm going to go talk to a friend.' Tom: 'Yeah, you go talk to your friend.' Rachel: 'Go tell him, Nice try.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has identified Tom as Danny's wingman and is dismissing him.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's self-satisfied 'Go tell him, Nice try' — delivered as if she's outwitted a chess grandmaster — is funny because she may have just catastrophically misread the situation.
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation on the Tom scene. Rachel's triumph feels hollow because we sense she's wrong — Tom was probably just a party guest. The confidence of 'Nice try' against what may be an innocent person is the ironic kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to act like I don't care at all. Like he means nothing to me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: *flips hair* 'Oh, hi. I didn't even notice you were here.'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: *yawns* 'You're leaving? Whatever.'

jokes.text: Rachel reports back to Monica: 'He just keeps lobbing them up and I keep knocking them right out of the park.' Monica: 'I think I need a drink.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is triumphant after dismissing Danny's supposed wingman.
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'I think I need a drink' is not support but exasperation — she's exhausted by Rachel's elaborate self-congratulatory sports metaphor spiral.
jokes.explanation: Monica's reaction is the punchline — she's not impressed, she's depleted. 'I think I need a drink' works because it's the audience surrogate response to Rachel's endless game-theory monologue. Good running gag button.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So, uh, how's the weather treating you?

dialogue.speaker: Danny
dialogue.line: It's... fine?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And you like... breathing? That's going well for you?

dialogue.speaker: Danny
dialogue.line: Why are you asking me this?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No reason! Do you enjoy having a face?

dialogue.speaker: Danny
dialogue.line: Monica, what is happening right now?

jokes.text: Chandler and Joey hiding in the apartment, counting to 100 before emerging to tell Ross they 'thought of a reason he should stay.' Ross appears first, tells them the application failed.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey had the apartment manager on the phone sabotaging Ross's application.
jokes.punchline: Ross appears before they're ready — they're mid-count-to-100. The elaborate guilty-conscience planning is interrupted by the very person they were plotting against.
jokes.explanation: The counting-to-100 bit is a nice visual (two grown men hiding and counting), and the juxtaposition of their guilty-conscience ritual with Ross's breezy return has comic value. The payoff on the sabotage arc is satisfying if not spectacular.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done playing games. I'm just going to tell him how I feel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's great, Mon. But what if he doesn't feel the same way?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Then I strike out. And you know what? That's okay. Because at least I stepped up to the plate.

jokes.text: Joey: 'You can't stay with Phoebe. We're roomies.' Ross protests they have no space. Joey gestures: 'We got plenty of space. There's still some by that speaker.'
jokes.setup: Ross says Phoebe offered her place; Joey insists they want him to stay.
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'plenty of space' is immediately qualified by pointing to a tiny sliver of space by the speaker — the gesture reveals how crowded the apartment actually is while he's selling it as spacious.
jokes.explanation: Funny visual contradiction — 'plenty of space' + 'some by that speaker' paints a clear picture of a crammed apartment. Joey's sincerity makes it land; he genuinely thinks this is a good offer.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So, uh, how about that weather we've been having?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's been... weather.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah. Very... weathey. I mean, weathery.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Mmhmm.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So do you, uh, like... pants?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Pants. You're wearing them. Are they... good pants?

jokes.text: Ross: 'So I'm a pimp, huh?' — referencing the sabotage call he apparently found out about.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey have just re-welcomed Ross; it's now apparent Ross knows about their sabotage (he was described as 'a big, tap-dancing pimp').
jokes.punchline: Ross's calm, slightly amused 'So I'm a pimp, huh?' shows he knows everything — and defuses the tension with self-deprecating acceptance.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. 'So I'm a pimp, huh?' is delivered with a tone that's knowing, slightly wounded, but forgiving — which makes it more touching and funnier than an angry response would be. The economy is superb — six words do enormous narrative and comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so Tom's been asking about my weekend plans, remembering details about my job, and he laughed at all my jokes at the party?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, he likes you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Or... he's working with you guys. This is a pity thing, right? You all got together and decided Rachel needs confidence so you hired this actor to pretend to like her?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Rachel, we didn't hire an actor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How much did you pay him? Because if it's under fifty dollars, he's really committed to the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: He just... likes you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm calling him right now and I'm asking him directly if this is some elaborate scheme you guys cooked up to make me feel better about myself.

jokes.text: 'So I'm a pimp, huh?'
jokes.setup: Ross stayed; in a quieter moment he confronts what his friends said about him.
jokes.punchline: Ross has found out about the reference call — his deadpan delivery of 'So I'm a pimp, huh?' is both a confrontation and an acceptance, delivered without real anger.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback delivery. 'So I'm a pimp, huh?' earns its laugh through understatement — Ross isn't furious, he's wearily resigned, which is both funnier and more character-true than outrage would be. The economy is near-perfect: five words that pay off the whole storyline and get a huge laugh. The juxtaposition of Ross — nerdy, earnest, divorced paleontologist — calmly asking if he's a pimp is inherently hilarious.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, I totally scored with him last night!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He was all over me. It was like I hit a home run or something.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you were at his apartment for five minutes to pick up your jacket.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Exactly! And he didn't even ask me to leave!

jokes.text: Ross promises to work on his 'annoying habits' — then the air purifier noise fills the room, and nothing changes.
jokes.setup: Ross sincerely vows to curb his annoying behaviors and make the living arrangement work.
jokes.punchline: The air purifier — the source of multiple complaints — immediately demonstrates that nothing will change. Ross either doesn't connect the dots or simply cannot stop.
jokes.explanation: A great visual/audio punchline — Ross's sincere promise is immediately contradicted by the purifier noise he's apparently unaware of. The joke needs no dialogue; the irony is structural. Good callback payoff for the air purifier running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You guys lied to me?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We can explain.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's fine. I'm calm.

jokes.text: Chandler, looking at Ross's new cowboy hat: 'The cowboy hat's a little much.' Ross: 'Come on, it's fun!'
jokes.setup: Ross has apparently been settling into the apartment and exploring new accessories.
jokes.punchline: Ross — the uptight, earnest paleontologist — is wearing a cowboy hat and defending it as 'fun,' which is very much at odds with his character.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual gag — Ross in a cowboy hat is inherently funny. The character dissonance does the work; the dialogue is minimal. Functions well as a scene-ender image.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What are you wearing?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm a knight! See, I have a sword and everything.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You look like you're going to a Renaissance faire.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So? Knights wore armor! This is historically accurate!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're in a fort made of couch cushions.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That doesn't make me any less of a knight!

jokes.text: Chandler picks up the cowboy hat: 'Isn't this a woman's hat?' Ross: 'Dude, stop talking crazy, and make us some tea!'
jokes.setup: Chandler tries on or examines the cowboy hat and notices it may be a woman's style.
jokes.punchline: Ross deflects with 'stop talking crazy' (dismissing a reasonable observation) and immediately pivots to demanding tea — revealing Ross has fully domesticated himself and is now ordering people around.
jokes.explanation: Great episode-ender character moment. 'Stop talking crazy and make us some tea!' is Ross at his most obliviously entitled — he's moved in, taken over, and is now hosting. The cowboy hat denial is a perfect non-answer. The switch from defensive to commanding is funny and very Ross-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why are you wearing a big ridiculous hat?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I could ask you the same thing.

tmdb_overview: Chandler and Joey let Ross move in with them once his marriage to Emily falls apart.  Meanwhile, Phoebe gets involved with the local health inspector and Rachel becomes convinced that Danny is trying to seduce her with mind games.
insight: Chandler's apartment debate generates 59 jokes in 22 minutes—solid density, modest payoff.
